rationale: A wins because it treats missing facts as tripwires, not confetti. Its line 'Partial disclosure kills this angle' is exactly the discipline this launch needs; B's 'Anker just set the timeline' is a grand claim standing on one company launch and a hope. B has usable bones, but it keeps stating the thesis before earning the evidence.
gaps_in_A: 'A profitable charger maker bets on a capital-heavy market' is the weakest included angle; the set admits 'the facts support only "large, profitable, publicly traded," which is a description, not a story.' Correct instinct, but then do not pretend it is ready material.

'The prevailing belief is that whole-home batteries mean panel work, transfer switches, and an electrician's week' imports unsourced category context. It may be true, but it is not in the update and should be framed as a reporting question, not a belief.

'Story type: trend' on the charger-to-house angle overlabels it. The copy later admits it is only a trend if Anker can supply comparable brand moves, so call it a company profile until the pattern exists.
gaps_in_B: 'Consumer electronics makers are moving from your pocket to your electrical panel' turns one Anker launch into a plural market movement. That is the kind of overreach that gets killed in the editor's second sentence.
'Anker just set the timeline' is empty swagger. The update gives no timeline data, adoption inflection, or proof Anker is setting anything beyond its own launch date.

'Anker is betting homeowners skip home batteries because of the installation job, not the price' invents Anker's theory of adoption. The facts say Anker claims no major rewiring; they do not say installation beats price as the barrier.
'The installation barrier has been cited repeatedly as the main friction point' and 'slower than solar's trajectory' are unsupported outside context. Useful if sourced, sloppy if smuggled in.
